nameStory: The 'Broad-tailed' part of this marine isopod's name comes from its distinctively wide, paddle-like tail section that's noticeably broader than most of its cousins. The 'Sevenbits' name refers to the seven distinct body segments visible along its back, each one looking like a separate armored plate or 'bit' fitted together like medieval chain mail.
description: The Broad-tailed Sevenbits is a small marine crustacean that looks like a flattened pill bug adapted for underwater life. These oval-shaped creatures typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a segmented body that appears armored. Unlike their terrestrial pill bug relatives, they can't roll into a ball, instead staying flat and using their swimming legs to dart through shallow coastal waters.

idTips.label: Broad tail section
idTips.description: The rear third of the body flares out noticeably wider than the front sections, like a tiny spatula or paddle - this broad tail feels firm and slightly rubbery to the touch

idTips.label: Seven body segments
idTips.description: Count the distinct armored plates along the back - there should be exactly seven segments that look like overlapping shields, each with a slight ridge you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Flattened oval shape
idTips.description: The entire body is compressed top-to-bottom, feeling like a firm, flexible disc rather than rounded like a terrestrial pill bug

idTips.label: Swimming legs
idTips.description: Flip it gently to see feathery, paddle-like swimming legs (pleopods) on the underside that feel soft and delicate, unlike the sturdy walking legs

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: The shell feels smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, without the bumpy or granular texture found on many other marine crustaceans

habitat: Look for Broad-tailed Sevenbits in shallow coastal waters along rocky shores and in tide pools from Massachusetts to Maine. They prefer areas with good water circulation around submerged rocks, kelp holdfasts, and among marine algae in depths of just a few feet to about 30 feet deep.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, often found clinging to the undersides of rocks in tide pools during low tide exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation time when they're most active and numerous, easily spotted swimming in shallow coastal waters and tide pools.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters, best found by turning over rocks and seaweed in tide pools.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they retreat to deeper waters and become less active in the cold, rarely seen during casual tide pool exploration.

funFact: Despite being crustaceans like lobsters and crabs, Broad-tailed Sevenbits can actually survive brief periods out of water by trapping moisture in their gill chambers - they're like tiny scuba divers carrying their own air supply for emergency surface visits!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other marine isopods, but remember 'broad tail, seven scales' - count those seven body segments and look for that distinctively wide tail section that's much broader than similar species.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertainty note: This species has very limited observation data in New England (only 2 records), so some details about local habitat preferences and seasonality are based on general knowledge of similar marine isopods and may not reflect this species' specific New England patterns.**
compareHints: Since this is the only Synidotea species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other marine isopods in the valvetail family by focusing on that signature broad tail - most related species have much narrower, more pointed tail sections. The combination of the seven distinct body segments plus that paddle-like wide tail makes it distinctive among New England's marine isopods.
